chapter.title: Your three accounts

cards.body: To shop in the bazaar you need three things: a **wallet, a runner, and a locker**. The wallet is your bank account, holding rupees. The runner is your broker, reached through a *trading account*, who carries your order to the stall. The locker sits at the bazaar gate, run not by your runner but by the bazaar itself, and every slice you buy is stored there under your name.
cards.simpler: Think of buying shares like shopping in a big market. You need three things: a **wallet, a runner, and a locker**. The wallet is your bank account, where your rupees live. The runner is your broker, whom you reach through a trading account. The runner carries your order to the shop. The locker sits at the market gate. The market itself runs it, not your runner. Every share you buy is kept there under your name.

cards.prompt: You bought 1 share of Infosys yesterday. Tonight your broker's app goes down for a week. Where is your share right now?

options.text: Inside the broker's app, out of reach until it comes back
In a locker run by the bazaar, untouched by the app outage
Back in your bank account as cash

whyNot.a: That's the runner, not the locker: the app only carries orders, it never stores shares.
whyNot.c: That's the wallet, not the locker: a bank holds rupees, never shares.

cards.reteach: The runner and the locker are different people. Your broker runs orders, but the share is written down in a locker kept by the bazaar, not by the broker. If the runner falls sick, the locker stays shut and yours.

cards.title: Three accounts, three jobs
cards.body:
The **bank account** you already have. It holds rupees and nothing else.

The *trading account* is opened with a *broker*, a firm licensed by SEBI to carry orders into the exchange. Money passes through it on the way to a purchase, and shares pass through it on the way to being sold. It is a corridor, not a room.

The *demat account* is the locker. Demat is short for dematerialised, meaning your shares exist as electronic entries, not paper. The locker is kept by one of two *depositories*, NSDL or CDSL. Your broker opens it for you, but the depository holds the keys.
cards.simpler: Your **bank account** holds rupees and nothing else. The trading account is opened with a broker, a firm licensed by SEBI to carry your orders into the exchange. Money passes through it when you buy. Shares pass through it when you sell. The demat account is the locker. Demat means your shares are electronic records, not paper. One of two depositories, NSDL or CDSL, keeps this locker. Your broker opens it, but the depository holds the keys.

cards.title: A text from a stranger
cards.body: Priya in Pune opens her accounts on a Tuesday night, on her phone, in about 15 minutes. On Wednesday she moves ₹5,000 from her bank into the trading account and buys 1 share of a Nifty 50 company at ₹2,400. On Thursday evening her phone buzzes: an SMS from CDSL, a name she has never heard, saying 1 share has been credited to her account. That is the locker speaking to her directly, skipping the runner. The leftover ₹2,600 sits in her trading account until she sends it back to the bank.
cards.simpler: Priya opens her accounts on Tuesday night, on her phone, in about 15 minutes. On Wednesday she moves ₹5,000 from her bank into the trading account and buys 1 share of a Nifty 50 company at ₹2,400. On Thursday evening an SMS arrives from CDSL. It says 1 share has been added to her account. That is **the locker speaking to her directly**, skipping the runner. The leftover ₹2,600 waits in her trading account until she moves it back.

cards.prompt: Rohan holds 12 shares. His broker's app is slow and he wants to switch brokers. Does he have to sell everything first?

options.text: Yes, the shares live in the broker's trading account and die with it
No, the shares sit in his demat at NSDL or CDSL and can be moved to a new demat without selling
No, the shares are already in his bank account, so nothing to move

whyNot.a: That's the runner, not the locker: a trading account never stores shares, so there is nothing in it to lose.
whyNot.c: That's the wallet, not the locker: a bank account cannot hold shares at all.

cards.reteach: Think of the broker as staff and the depository as the building. You can change staff without emptying your locker. Shares are moved from one demat to another by a transfer form, no selling needed.

cards.title: Getting the keys, and what they cost
cards.body:
Before any broker opens your accounts, SEBI makes them do *KYC*, Know Your Customer, a check on who you are. You need your **PAN card**, which is your tax ID, your Aadhaar for address and an electronic signature, a bank proof such as a statement or cancelled cheque, and a selfie. Most brokers finish this on a phone, and the accounts go live in 1 to 2 working days.

Charges to look for: an account-opening fee, which many brokers have dropped to zero, and a yearly demat maintenance fee, often a few hundred rupees. Per-trade charges come in chapter 4. Check the broker's name on SEBI's website before you sign anything.
cards.simpler: Before a broker opens your accounts, SEBI makes them run KYC, a check on who you are. You need your **PAN card**, your tax ID, plus Aadhaar for address and e-signature, a bank proof, and a selfie. Most brokers do it on a phone. Accounts go live in 1 to 2 working days. Fees: an opening fee, often zero, and a yearly demat fee, often a few hundred rupees. Check the broker's name on SEBI's website before signing.

cards.body: Arjun moved ₹40,000 into his trading account in March "to be ready" and never bought anything. In August it was still there, earning nothing, while his bank savings account would have paid him interest. Spot it: money parked in the corridor instead of the wallet. SEBI even makes brokers push idle cash back to your bank every few months, which tells you how it is meant to be used.
cards.simpler: Arjun moved ₹40,000 into his trading account in March, to be ready. He never bought anything. In August the money was still sitting there, earning nothing. In his bank savings account it would have earned interest. The mistake: **money parked in the hallway instead of the wallet**. SEBI makes brokers send idle cash back to your bank every few months. That tells you how the trading account is meant to be used: as a pass-through, not a parking spot.

cards.prompt: Match the three jobs. Which line is right?

options.text: Bank holds cash, trading account places orders, demat holds shares
Bank holds cash, demat places orders, trading account holds shares
Trading account holds cash and shares, demat places orders, bank is unused

whyNot.b: Runner and locker swapped: demat is the locker that stores, trading is the runner that orders.
whyNot.c: That gives the corridor the storage job: a trading account holds nothing for long, and the bank is where cash lives.

cards.reteach: One sentence each. Wallet: bank, rupees. Runner: trading account, carries orders to the exchange. Locker: demat, keeps the shares at NSDL or CDSL.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Your bank is the wallet, your trading account is the runner who carries orders, and your demat is the locker at NSDL or CDSL where **every share you own actually sits**. The broker opens all three for you after KYC with PAN and Aadhaar, but the broker never holds your shares.
cards.simpler: Your bank is the wallet. Your trading account is the runner who carries your orders. Your demat account is the locker at NSDL or CDSL, where **every share you own actually sits**. The broker opens all three for you after KYC, using your PAN and Aadhaar. But the broker never holds your shares.

cards.body: Tonight, open the SEBI website and search the registered intermediaries list for the broker you are considering. Already have an account? Find your demat number: 16 digits means CDSL, starting with IN means NSDL.
cards.simpler: Tonight, open the SEBI website and look up the registered intermediaries list. Search for the broker you are thinking of using. If the name is there, the broker is registered with SEBI. Already have an account? Find your **demat number**: 16 digits means CDSL, and one starting with IN means NSDL.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now open a demat and trading account and say which account holds your shares and which holds your cash.
